text: The announcement has the Portland Public
School District facing a lot of
questions and some significant
criticism.
>> In an exclusive interview, Fox 12's Pete
Ferryman had a chance to sit down with
Dr. Kimberly Armstrong, the district
superintendent, to talk about the plan
and to address many of the questions
from parents.
>> So, no shortage of challenges with your
position, right?
>> Right.
>> She walked into a tough situation when
she took the job and it just got
tougher. The recommended school closure
list has sparked anger with at least one
rally already planned for Tuesday night.
The strong pushback raising questions
about whether the plan might be dead on
arrival politically.
>> And the way I explained it um to one
student, it's like, you know, you're
going to a fair and you have a set um
a budget and you have uh six people with
you. Uh the amount that you spend is
going to be vastly different if you have
three people to spend on.
>> Do you think that you have the votes for
this to get it through the school board?
What I'm hearing is that I mean, the
outcry from the public already, before
they've even seen the details, is
significant. Are you confident? Do you
have the horses for this?
>> Well, I'm confident that they're ready
to engage in conversation about
sustainability. We expect feedback,
pushback, comments, questions. We
welcome it.
>> Dr. Kimberly Armstrong says the biggest
factor is declining enrollment and has
labeled their school closure plan
right-sizing.
>> Explain to me what right-sizing
really means.
>> Yeah. So, I would say simply, it's about
getting to the right size in the um
portfolio of schools that we have.
>> A school board member asked recently how
many layoffs this will create. Do you
have that number yet?
>> I don't have that number and a lot of
people are wanting us to put that math
with the um the closure plan and what I
tell them is that the state school fund
is set by the governor and uh she will
release that.
>> Meanwhile, many questioned the
district's record of financial
management. Even when adjusted for
inflation, the district is spending
about 23% more per student than 10 years
ago. Armstrong says since she came
aboard, they've tried to tackle the
budget deficits, reducing staffing in
the central office by 14%, but public
frustration remains high.
>> You did receive a significant raise, and
there's been some pushback regarding
that. Do you want to set the record
straight as far as
if you feel that that was justified?
>> Yeah, I appreciate that question. And I
think there's some misconception in
that, right?
My employment agreement was negotiated
upon my hire back in 2024, and was under
current market rate. And so, while it
made the news several months ago, the
rate and the raise was determined back
in 2024. What I did ask for, though, is
that my COLA be capped.
>> If you're a parent or a student, and
your school is on this list, what kind
of data would they need to provide to
you in order to get themselves off the
list?
>> Yeah. Well, first I will say that we do
want to spend the month of October
engaged in public discussion. We'll be
out to school sites, impacted sites.
We want to continue to have listening
sessions, both virtual and in-person,
and with our school board. So, there'll
be many opportunities to give input.
>> Do you foresee the possibility that
that the parent input or the student
input might lead to changes in the list,
or is it strictly performative?
>> Yeah. That's a great question, and we
actually expect it to lead to changes.
>> Armstrong says it's also very possible
that the board will decide to pause the
plan and address it at a later date. In
the meantime, we have a link to the full
conversation with Dr. Armstrong on our
Fox 12 News app.
